section_summary: This section traces U.S. diplomatic, consular, military-intelligence, and export-control reporting on Japanese aviation from 1932 through 1939. It covers Japanese air operations at Shanghai and in China, proposed or actual transfers of American and European aircraft and technology, aviation-related materials and factories, prospective air bases, and Japanese aircraft performance. Much of the section consists of cross-reference sheets directing readers to documents filed elsewhere, alongside correspondence over the Glenn L. Martin BM-2 bomber, Mitsubishi engine parts, the Flying Flea, and a reported Japanese light-metal plant.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese flights over the Shanghai Settlement
subfiles.about: Records a telegram concerning Japanese aircraft flying over the Shanghai International Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to telegram 78 of February 19, 1932: Japanese practice flights over the Shanghai Settlement would stop unless absolutely necessary.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 78 on flights over the Shanghai Settlement
subfiles.about: Reports Japan's qualified promise to stop military aircraft from flying over the Shanghai Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 78: Japan replied aviators were told not to fly over the Settlement but kept an exception for flights indispensable to defense or protecting Japanese lives, less satisfactory than an oral assurance to Admiral Taylor.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on accidental Japanese bombing in the Settlement
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that Japanese bombing in the Settlement resulted from defective bomb racks.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Shanghai telegram 76: Japan says the Settlement bombing was accidental, caused by defective bomb racks.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 76 on Japanese firing and bombing in Shanghai
subfiles.about: Transmits Japan's explanation and apology for machine-gun fire and accidental bomb release in the Settlement.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 76: Japanese naval headquarters says aviators fired believing the site outside the American defense area, blames a defective bomb rack, expresses regret and promises precautions.

subfiles.title: Note on Dutch East Indies bauxite for Japanese aircraft production
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese agreement to obtain bauxite from Bintan Island for aluminum and aircraft production.
subfiles.summary: A Japanese company with Formosa aluminum works reportedly agreed to take 24,000 tons of bauxite yearly from the Nibam Company on Bintan Island, for Japan's air fleet.

subfiles.title: Confidential note on alleged physiological limitations of Japanese aviators
subfiles.about: Indexes an allegation that anatomical differences supposedly prevented Japanese pilots from attaining the highest ability.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a confidential report asserting a now-discredited racialized claim that Japanese ear-canal defects made elite aviation impossible.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on possible German aviation aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch concerning possible German aircraft materials or instructors for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: possible German agreement to supply Japan aircraft materials or instructors, though German factories and pilots were busy with Germany's own air resources.

subfiles.title: Note on proposed Japanese manufacture of Triangle parachutes
subfiles.about: Records departmental approval for foreign sale and manufacture of Triangle Parachute Equipment and Japanese interest in production rights.
subfiles.summary: War and Navy Departments had no objection to foreign manufacture of Triangle parachutes; Mitsubishi Shoji sought manufacturing rights for the Japanese Empire after Mikuni Shoten raised interest.

subfiles.title: Note on export of Lear-O-Scope direction finders
subfiles.about: Indexes a request to ship Lear-O-Scope radio direction finders to Japan and Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Charles H. Payne requested government permission to export the Lear-O-Scope radio direction finder. The intended destinations were Japan and Mexico.

subfiles.title: Glenn L. Martin request concerning sale of BM-2 bomber designs
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Requests a government policy ruling on selling BM-2 dive-bomber design data and a manufacturing license to Japanese representatives.
subfiles.summary: Glenn L. Martin's Hartson says Japanese representatives want drawings and rights for the former Navy BM-2 dive bomber; he argues the Navy has lost interest and seeks a formal government statement.

subfiles.title: Referral of the BM-2 proposal to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Asks the Navy what reply should be given to Glenn L. Martin's proposed sale of BM-2 designs to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Moore sends the Navy Secretary Martin's September 20 request on selling BM-2 design data and a license to Japan and asks the appropriate response.

subfiles.title: Interim reply to the Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the BM-2 request and advises that it has been referred to the Navy.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Martin's September 20 letter on BM-2 data and rights, saying the Navy Secretary has the question and a further reply will follow.

subfiles.title: Glenn L. Martin request for expedited BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Requests prompt action because a Japanese purchasing party was expected to visit on October 11.
subfiles.summary: Hartson follows up on the BM-2 request and asks an early decision, as a Japanese party planned to visit the company October 11.

subfiles.title: Second interim reply on the BM-2 proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises that the Navy had not yet decided whether the BM-2 contained secret military equipment.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges the September 30 follow-up; the Navy hasn't reported whether the BM-2 has secret equipment, and he will write when it answers.

subfiles.title: Navy objection to releasing BM-2 designs to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports War and Navy Department opposition to selling BM-2 design data and manufacturing rights to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Navy returns Martin's BM-2 request; the War and Navy Departments object because release would prejudice military secrets and national defense.

subfiles.title: Copy of State Department referral to the Navy
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Reproduces the State Department's request for Navy guidance on the BM-2 sale proposal.
subfiles.summary: Copy of Moore's referral to the Navy: Japanese representatives want BM-2 design data and a license, and he asks what to tell Martin.

subfiles.title: Copy of Glenn L. Martin's BM-2 request
subfiles.from: J. T. Hartson, Glenn L. Martin Company
subfiles.about: Reproduces the company's case for permission to sell BM-2 drawings and manufacturing rights to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Copy of Martin's request: Japanese interest in making the BM-2 or similar dive bombers, unordered since 1933, of no Navy interest and otherwise idle.

subfiles.title: Final rejection of the BM-2 sale proposal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Informs the company that the War and Navy Departments opposed release of the BM-2 material.
subfiles.summary: Green conveys the Navy's answer: the government objects because releasing BM-2 data and the license would endanger military secrets and national defense.

subfiles.title: Notification to the Acting Secretary of War on the BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Harry H. Woodring, Acting Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Provides the War Department with a copy of the rejection sent to the Glenn L. Martin Company.
subfiles.summary: Moore informs Woodring of State's response on the Japanese BM-2 proposal, enclosing a copy of the letter to the company.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to the Secretary of the Navy on the BM-2 decision
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Navy's objection and encloses the State Department's reply to Glenn L. Martin.
subfiles.summary: Moore acknowledges the Navy's October 29 decision on the Japanese purchase and encloses the rejection sent to Martin.

subfiles.title: Mitsubishi inquiry about export licenses for aircraft-engine parts
subfiles.from: Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha, Ltd., New York
subfiles.about: Asks whether licenses were required for two imminent shipments of aircraft-engine parts and requests additional application forms.
subfiles.summary: Mitsubishi plans November 29-30 departures from New York and San Francisco, encloses license applications, and asks whether aircraft-engine parts need licenses since customs thought not; it requests forms and updated regulations.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on aircraft-engine-part licenses
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Advises Mitsubishi that no license was required to export aircraft-engine parts to Japan.
subfiles.summary: State says aircraft-engine parts need no export license under its arms regulations, rejects and returns Mitsubishi's two applications, and supplies twenty blank forms.

subfiles.title: Despatch on midget airplanes in Japan
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese manufacture, importation, military use, and subsidization of Flying Flea light aircraft.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports a factory for the French Flying Flea, an aviator's claim that forty imported ones serve in Japan, an Army trainer designation, and a 1,000-yen subsidy for domestic purchasers.

subfiles.title: Japan Advertiser excerpt on the Flying Flea subsidy
subfiles.about: Reports a ¥1,000 subsidy for purchasers of low-powered airplanes manufactured in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Japan Advertiser: the Imperial Aeronautical Society approved a subsidy for Japanese aircraft with engines up to fifty horsepower, mainly the Flying Flea, cutting its price to about 2,600 yen; a third-class license needs ten solo hours.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on expansion of Japanese naval aviation
subfiles.about: Indexes a report on planned increases in aircraft carriers, auxiliary vessels, and the Japanese naval air force.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch 1953: a naval program for the coming year with more carriers, auxiliaries and a larger naval air force.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on rumored German-Italian aviation aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram about rumors of secret German and Italian technical and material assistance to Japanese aviation.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a rumored German-Japanese agreement in Tokyo with a secret clause giving German and Italian technical and material aid, especially for aviation.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 235 on the German-Japanese agreement
subfiles.about: Reports diplomatic information and rumors concerning the German-Japanese agreement and possible aviation assistance.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 235: neither Japan's Foreign Office nor the German Embassy denied negotiations but denied a formal agreement; rumors say Italy joined, Poland declined, and secret German and Italian aviation aid would shorten Japan's replenishment program; the Privy Council reportedly considers it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Pratas Reef and Japanese air-base plans
subfiles.about: Indexes a London telegram about Japanese occupation of Pratas Reef and possible air-base construction.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: British and French concern over Japan's occupation of Pratas Reef, its weather station's dismantling and a planned air base, with a proposed joint demarche in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Telegram no. 593 on Japanese island occupations and air bases
subfiles.about: Reports British and French concern over Japanese moves at Pratas, Hainan, and the Paracels and asks what action the United States contemplated.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 593: Britain reports Japan occupied Pratas Reef, dismantled its weather station and plans an air base, with secret word of an attack on Hainan; Britain and France plan a joint Tokyo demarche and hope the U.S. will make similar representations.

subfiles.title: Handwritten abstract on Japanese pursuit aircraft over Shiuchow
subfiles.about: Summarizes reports of unusually capable Japanese pursuit aircraft raiding the Shiuchow airplane factory.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten abstract: Japanese pursuit planes secretly joined raids on a Guangdong aircraft factory, with remarkable climb, speed and maneuverability; the factory had completed a run of aircraft.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the performance of Japanese pursuit planes
subfiles.from: Addison E. Southard, American Consul General, Hong Kong
subfiles.about: Relays Charles Healy Day's eyewitness account of advanced Japanese fighters attacking the Shiuchow Aircraft Works.
subfiles.summary: Day reports Japanese retractable-gear monoplanes decisively outperformed Chinese Hawk II and III fighters, above 280 mph and 3,000 feet per minute, with severe Chinese losses; Southard adds the factory might move north toward Hankou.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Italian airplanes and pilots sent to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a despatch transmitting a military attaché report on Italian aircraft and pilots sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to despatch 862: shipment of Italian airplanes and pilots to Japan.

subfiles.title: Ithaca reader's inquiry about American aircraft exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Asks the Department to explain a newspaper image of American warplanes being shipped to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Knott, an Ithaca mother, encloses a clipping on aircraft exports to explain to her eleven-year-old son, distressed by the arms trade.

subfiles.title: Ithaca Journal clipping: America Sends War Planes to Japan
subfiles.about: Shows an American fighting aircraft being loaded at Los Angeles for shipment to Japan and criticizes continuing trade during the war in China.
subfiles.summary: Ithaca Journal clipping: American planes are a common export to Japan amid debate on neutrality law, and Senator Nye says the bombs that sank the Panay were probably American-made.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on alleged Seversky aircraft production for Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes informant information that Seversky planned to manufacture and ship twenty advanced aircraft to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: a Justice informant alleges Seversky at Farmingdale built twenty large aircraft for Japan that outperform U.S. fighters.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on restricting aircraft sales to belligerents
subfiles.about: Suggests that voluntary restrictions on aircraft sales should apply to Germany and Italy as well as Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Scott answers the Secretary's suggestion on aircraft sales to bombing governments, recommending adding Germany and Italy and forwarding a letter proposing Neutrality Act revision.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese aircraft purchases in the United States
subfiles.about: Indexes a telegram reporting export licenses for fourteen aircraft and prospective Japanese purchases of many more bombers.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: licenses for fourteen planes issued June 9, and Japanese interests approached a U.S. company about buying many bombers at once.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Heinkel bombers shipped to Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes a report that four Heinkel He 111 bombers were observed aboard a Japanese steamer bound for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: an American Army officer saw four Heinkel 111 bombers on a Japanese ship, shipped from Germany to Japan.

subfiles.title: Departmental routing note concerning the Austrian magnesium report
subfiles.about: Asks whether the report on an aviation-related Japanese light-metal plant should be sent to naval intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary routing note on the Austrian magnesium report, asking if it merits forwarding to Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Letter on a reported Japanese light-metal plant
subfiles.from: Eliot B. Coulter, American Consul General, Beirut
subfiles.about: Transmits Ernst Gutman's information that an Austrian magnesium firm helped establish a similar aviation-metal plant in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gutman says Japanese technicians visited the firm's Radenthein plant after anti-Nazi director Konrad Erdmann was removed, and the firm helped set up a Japanese light-metal plant for aircraft without American president Emil Winter's knowledge; Coulter finds him credible.

subfiles.title: Reply to the American Consul General at Beirut
subfiles.to: Eliot B. Coulter, American Consul General, Beirut
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report on the Japanese light-metal plant and states that it was forwarded to the War and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: Murray thanks the Beirut consul general for the February 21 information from the former Austrian consul in Damascus, sent to both military departments.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese light-metal report to the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards excerpts from the Beirut report to the Office of Naval Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: State sends the Navy excerpts on a planned Japanese light-metal aircraft plant; the sole booklet and map went to the War Department.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese light-metal report to the War Department
subfiles.about: Forwards the Beirut report, booklet, and maps to the Military Intelligence Division.
subfiles.summary: State sends the War Department excerpts on the Japanese light-metal plant with the only booklet and maps; the Navy gets only the excerpts.
